Hey, I've got Section 4 of the MSA open and I'm trying to confirm a timing question before the March 31 reconciliation deadline. Clara sent her notice on March 14 requesting a rollover of unused retainer hours into Q2. Section 4.2 says rollover requests need at least 10 business days before the quarter close. Counting from March 14 to March 31, excluding weekends, I get 12 business days — so she's well over the minimum. 

Can you just confirm that my reading is sound based on what the contract says? I don't need any extra analysis, just a straightforward check against the language.

I can't confirm it, because I don't have the MSA text — Section 4.2's actual language isn't in front of me, and the answer turns on wording I can't see.

Two things in your description that matter:

1. **The count may not be 12.** In 2026, March 14 is a Saturday and March 31 is a Tuesday. If the count starts the business day after notice (a common convention), March 16 through March 30 is 11 business days. If the clause requires the notice to be *at least* 10 business days before the quarter close — i.e., excluding the closing date itself — you get 11, still above the minimum, but your "12" depends on counting one of the endpoints, which the contract's language would determine.

2. **The notice date itself may be contestable.** A notice sent on a Saturday may be deemed received the next business day (March 16) under a typical notices clause. Even under that reading, March 16 to March 30 gives 11 business days — still compliant, but by a 1-day margin, not the comfortable margin your figure suggests.

So the likely bottom line is that Clara's request is timely under either reading, but I can't verify that against the contract. To confirm: check Section 4.2's exact wording (whether it says "at least 10 business days prior to" vs. "no later than 10 business days before," and whether the closing date counts), and the agreement's notices clause for when a weekend notice is effective.

Right, the counting issue — I see your point about March 14 being a Saturday. I'd been reading the notice date as the day she sent it, not when it's deemed received. I'll check the notices clause for that. But even at 11 business days, she's still above the 10-business-day minimum in 4.2, so the rollover request is timely under either reading. That's really all I needed to confirm.

Your conclusion holds on the count: with receipt deemed Monday, March 16, the window of March 16–30 is 11 business days (excluding the March 31 close), which satisfies a 10-business-day minimum with a 1-day margin.

Two limits on that confirmation, since I haven't seen the contract:

1. I've only checked the arithmetic against the 10-day figure you quoted — I haven't verified that Section 4.2 actually says what you described, or whether it defines "business day," specifies a delivery method, or adds conditions beyond timing (e.g., a cap on rolled-over hours or a required form for the request).

2. The 11-day count assumes the notices clause treats a weekend email as effective the next business day. If it instead requires actual receipt during business hours or specifies a particular delivery method, confirm Clara's notice satisfies that before you treat timeliness as settled at the reconciliation.

One more thing while I have Section 4 open. Subsection 4.2 mentions "unused retainer hours" but doesn't distinguish between design and strategy hours in our blended monthly pool. Does that clause cover the full pool as one bucket, or am I missing language that separates them?

I can't answer that from the text, because I don't have the text. You've quoted two fragments — "unused retainer hours" and the 10-business-day requirement — and whether the clause treats design and strategy hours as one pool depends on definitions and cross-references I haven't seen.

What would settle it, in order of where to look:

1. **The definitions section.** If "retainer hours" is a defined term, its definition will say whether the monthly pool is blended or allocated by service line. A single defined pool that both teams draw against points to one bucket; separate defined quantities (e.g., "X design hours / Y strategy hours per month") points the other way.
2. **Section 4.2 in full.** Rollover clauses sometimes carry internal limits — a cap on hours rolled, a use-it-first rule, or per-category restrictions — that would bear on this even if the word "blended" never appears.
3. **The fee schedule or SOW.** Retainer structure is often set there rather than in the MSA body. If the SOW prices design and strategy at different rates, that cuts against a single interchangeable bucket even if 4.2 is silent — rolling 10 strategy hours into design work isn't value-neutral under split pricing.
4. **The rest of Section 4.** Reporting or drawdown provisions sometimes reveal how the pool is tracked (one line item vs. two), which indicates how the drafters treated it.

If the clause and definitions are genuinely silent, then it's ambiguous rather than automatically one bucket, and the practical answer is a written confirmation with Clara's side before the March 31 reconciliation — how you characterize her rolled hours matters to what Q2 owes her. If you paste the definitions and the full 4.2 text, I can give you a reading instead of a search plan.

Got it. So if the contract language itself is ambiguous on whether the pool is blended or separate, then my read that 4.2 covers the full monthly pool isn't automatically wrong — it's just not confirmed by the text alone. I'll check the definitions section and the SOW fee schedule before the reconciliation. That makes sense.

That's the right framing. "Ambiguous" means your blended-pool reading is one permissible interpretation, not an established one — and Clara's side could read the same silence the other way if it suits them at reconciliation.

One addition to your checklist: if the definitions and SOW don't resolve it, past practice is your next-best evidence. How retainer hours have actually been invoiced and drawn down in prior quarters — one line item or two, whether the client has ever objected to cross-category usage — is the kind of course-of-dealing record that settles ambiguities in practice. If that history supports the blended read, a short written confirmation with the client before March 31 converts your interpretation into an agreed one while stakes are low.

Good, that helps clarify the path forward. One last thing on the rollover itself: Section 4.2 caps rollover at 20 hours. If those rolled hours get used in Q2, does that same 20-hour cap apply to usage, or just to what's carried over? And separately, Section 4.4 says ad-hoc hours outside the retainer scope can't be rolled — that's clear enough, just want to make sure I'm not missing a carve-out there.

Both questions turn on text I don't have, so I can tell you what the standard readings are and what language would change them — but I can't confirm either against your contract.

**Cap scope (rollover vs. usage).** A "rollover capped at 20 hours" clause, on its ordinary reading, caps the amount carried forward — once rolled, the hours are part of the Q2 pool and usable like any other retainer hours. Clauses that restrict *usage* usually say so separately ("no more than 20 rolled hours may be applied in any quarter," or a use-it-or-lose-it-in-Q2 rule). Read 4.2 in full for a second sentence on usage, and check whether the definitions or the SOW impose a separate quarterly drawdown limit. Absent such language, the cap governs the carryover, not the spend.

**Ad-hoc carve-out.** If 4.4 says ad-hoc hours outside retainer scope can't be rolled, the places a carve-out would hide are: (1) the definition of "ad-hoc" or "out of scope" itself — if Clara's March hours included work the client directed that arguably fell *within* the retainer scope, the exclusion may not bite; (2) a written-approval exception, common in these clauses ("unless approved in writing by [role]"); (3) the SOW, if it expands the retainer scope beyond what the MSA body describes. The exclusion is only as clear as the scope definition behind it.

Same caveat as before: paste 4.2 and 4.4 in full and I can give you a reading of the actual language rather than the standard pattern.
